claims.text: Local chemical heterogeneity and variations in short-range order induce spatial fluctuations in stacking or shear fault energies.
Spatial fluctuations in fault energy govern dislocation slip, twinning, and pinning.
The effects of local chemical heterogeneity on dislocation dynamics control alloy strength and deformation behavior.
CoCrFeNi, CoCrFeMnNi, and NiCoCr-based alloys can contain local chemical-order variations despite nominally uniform overall compositions.
Fabrication route, cooling rate, heat treatment, and cold working can deliberately modulate local chemical heterogeneity and short-range order.
Atom probe tomography and high-resolution STEM can quantify the relevant local chemical variations and fault-energy distributions.
Differences in local chemical ordering and compositional fluctuations produce spatial variations in stacking or shear fault energy.
Heterogeneous fault-energy landscapes modulate activation barriers for dislocation motion.
Heterogeneous fault-energy landscapes promote combined slip and twinning or intermittent dislocation pinning.
The combined deformation mechanisms caused by local variations delay failure and enhance mechanical properties relative to a chemically homogeneous baseline.
Samples with greater local chemical heterogeneity will have higher yield strengths than samples with a more uniform fault-energy distribution.
Samples with greater local chemical heterogeneity will have greater ductility than samples with a more uniform fault-energy distribution.
The increased strength and ductility will correlate with combined slip, twinning, and dislocation pinning, including wavy or jumpy dislocation paths.
Alloys processed to minimize local chemical-order variations will exhibit more conventional dislocation slip.
Alloys processed to minimize local chemical-order variations will have lower yield strength and ductility.
The proposed relationship should hold from room temperature to approximately 500 K under otherwise controlled mechanical-test conditions.
Grain size and residual stress may also influence fault-energy distributions or mechanical behavior and therefore confound attribution to chemical heterogeneity.

The hypothesis is falsified if no statistically significant correlation is observed between local chemical heterogeneity, fault-energy variation, deformation mechanisms, and mechanical performance relative to the homogenized baseline.
